content: A mirror image is a duplicate of an object or figure created by reflection in a mirror. In two-dimensional geometry, the mirror image of an object is a virtual image formed by reflection in a plane mirror. This image is identical in size to the original object but differs in orientation unless the object has reflection symmetry, also known as P-symmetry. For example, if a point on an object has coordinates (x, y, z), its mirror image, reflected across the y-z plane, will have coordinates (-x, y, z). This means that the reflection reverses the coordinate axis perpendicular to the mirror's surface. Importantly, a mirror image does not reverse left and right or up and down; instead, it reverses front and back. Two-dimensional mirror images can be observed in mirrors, reflective surfaces, or printed materials viewed from the reverse side. In three dimensions, the concept of a mirror image extends to three-dimensional objects, including their internal structures, even if these structures are not visible. This type of mirror image is referred to as an enantiomer or enantiomorph. A three-dimensional mirror image appears to have depth and changes as the observer moves, due to the shifting relative positions of objects in the reflection. Observing a mirror from different positions, while remaining on one side of the mirror, is equivalent to viewing the three-dimensional mirror image of the space on that side. Without additional mirrors, only the half-space in front of the mirror is relevant. However, if another mirror is introduced, the mirror image of the other half-space becomes visible as well. Mirror images have practical applications. For instance, text is sometimes intentionally displayed as a mirror image so it can be read correctly when viewed through a mirror. Additionally, some movie theaters use a Rear Window Captioning System, which employs mirror images to provide captions for individuals with hearing impairments. When two mirrors are positioned at an angle (α) to each other, the reflections create a visual effect as if the world has been rotated by an angle of 2α. This effect is observed when looking through the intersection of the two half-spaces defined by the mirrors. The field of view is determined by the edges of the mirrors. For example, if the mirrors have vertical edges, the left edge of the field of view corresponds to the plane formed by the right edge of the first mirror and the right edge of the second mirror, which appears on the left in the mirror image. In the case of two parallel mirrors, looking through both mirrors once creates the appearance of a world that has been translated by twice the distance between the mirrors. This translation occurs in the direction perpendicular to the mirrors, away from the observer. Since the observer looks at the mirrors at an oblique angle, the translation also includes a perpendicular component. This shifted view can alternatively be described as a translation of the observer in the opposite direction. For example, in a vertical periscope, the world appears shifted away from the observer and downward by the length of the periscope. However, it is often more practical to describe this as the observer being shifted upward and backward by the same distance.
